1:
Two determinations stand behind the voyage. Gill sees three concurring — the decree of God made known to Paul, his own resolution upon it, which was why he appealed, and the sentence of Festus, settling the time as well. Henry puts it more sharply: it was determined by the counsel of God before the counsel of Festus, for whatever men intended God had work for him at Rome. Calvin thinks Luke records the sea journey chiefly to show that Paul was brought to Rome by the hand of God, whose glory appeared even on the way, so that the journey confirmed his apostleship; and he marks that though Paul is handed over with other prisoners, the Lord will soon put a great difference between him and the evil-doers bound beside him. Henry hears in that company an old note, Paul linked with malefactors as Christ was with the thieves, since it is no new thing for the innocent to be numbered with transgressors — and observes that later these men nearly cost him his life, while for his sake they kept theirs.

The pronoun is disputed and revealing. Gill reports that the Latin, Syriac and Arabic read he and the Ethiopic reads Paul outright, but the Greek copies read we; Barnes finds them uniform in that and takes the word as proof that Luke was of the party, though whether at his own charge or the government's is not said. Robertson calls the construction awkward Greek, an infinitive of the kind the Greek Old Testament uses for a Hebrew form, and judges that the detail and accuracy of this narrative throw more light on ancient seafaring than all other sources together — yet its author, exact as he is with sea terms, writes like a landsman and not a sailor. Of the guard, Ellicott sets out three accounts of the Augustan band: that it was levied at Sebaste, where Sebastene cavalry is known; that it answers to the equestrian young men whom Nero had lately formed into a claque and named Augustani, which he thinks likeliest; or that its officer is the Julius Priscus later made a prefect of the praetorian cohorts. Clarke reports the name found on an ancient marble, Barnes takes it for a division named in the emperor's honour, Calvin guesses at the old praetorian band, and Robertson confesses we do not know, suggesting the imperial grain service.

The other prisoners and the ship raise smaller questions. Ellicott holds that the word for other implies a different class, and supposes they too had appealed, since otherwise there was no object in sending them to Rome; Robertson thinks them condemned men bound for the shows. On the port Gill argues for an African Adrumetum built by Tyrians, whose Phoenician name he renders the court of death, from bad air or a dangerous haven; Clarke reports that guess and rejects it for the Mysian town opposite Mitylene, which the others assume. Ellicott adds that there was little direct traffic between Caesarea and Rome, so the passage had to be made in one vessel after another, and dates the embarkation to late August, reckoning back from the Fast; Robertson calls it a coaster going home for the winter. Ellicott infers that Aristarchus had waited out the two years in Palestine and meant only to return to Thessalonica. Calvin, noticing that many went up to Jerusalem and two remain, will not blame the absent, who may have been hindered or dismissed, but praises this man as rich enough to bear three years of charges away from home, and crossing the sea after an imprisonment to serve at Rome under many reproaches. Wesley says only that he and Luke went by choice, not ashamed of his bonds; Robertson notes Ramsay's suggestion that they travelled as slaves, friends not being permitted, but thinks Luke got leave as his physician.
3:
The courtesy at Sidon is noticed by everyone. Ellicott and Robertson point out that the adverb is literally philanthropically, the one adding this to the other instances where officials thought well of Paul, the other that Julius was kind to him throughout. The leave granted is read two ways. Ellicott renders the phrase as availing himself of their care and thinks it a provision of clothing and comforts, welcome after two years in custody; Robertson allows it may have been hospitality but wonders whether medical attention was needed after so long a confinement. Barnes recalls that Felix had allowed the same, and supposes a man who passed that way so often had friends in every principal city; Robertson notes that this is Paul's first visit, though there were Christians in Phoenicia already. Clarke traces it to the impression made on Agrippa and Festus, and guesses that the soldier chained to his arm fared well on his account; Wesley thinks Julius may have heard the defence. Calvin turns it into a duty: Paul could have hidden in so large a city, but was bound by the oracle and could not withdraw from his calling; and since the centurion, who might have left him in the stench of the ship, had let him go to friends, he could not have saved his own life at that man's peril without treachery — nor may we let anyone suffer for having treated us kindly.

From Sidon the winds govern everything. Barnes explains that to sail under Cyprus is to hug its coast, keeping the island between the ship and the westerlies. Ellicott makes the wind north-west and has them take the channel between Cyprus and Cilicia, sheltered as far as the promontory now called Capo Andrea; Robertson names these winds Etesian. Clarke reports the many spellings of Myra and Grotius's conjecture that all are corrupt for Limyra; Ellicott calls it a former metropolis with a theatre and aqueduct still standing; Robertson adds that no disciples are named here, nor at Lasea, Melita or Syracuse. Of the ship they found there, Gill reports that the top sail was the mark of an Alexandrian, no others being allowed to spread one or obliged to strike it in port. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott agree it was a corn ship of the Egyptian trade blown out of its course, and Ellicott that such traders avoided the African coast for fear of the Syrtis, the change of plan sparing a landing in Mysia and a journey overland.

The slow passage west is measured out in miles. Ellicott reckons that in many days — a fortnight or three weeks — they had not made the hundred and twenty miles from Myra to Cnidus, the Etesian gales blowing through August; Robertson makes it a hundred and thirty and marks Cnidus as the point where the land's protection ceased, the verb for sailing slowly occurring nowhere else in scripture. Clarke adds the heavy lading to the contrary wind, which Gill takes from the Syriac. Ellicott explains the decision: with the coast trending north there was no making head against such a wind, so the only course was south for the lee of Crete, reached at Cape Salmone. On the anchorage they differ. Barnes doubts it was a harbour at all and calls it an open road which an old geographer named the fair shore; Ellicott and Robertson fix it two miles east of Cape Matala, the latter adding that it is no place to winter. Lasea has vanished. Clarke finds no such city and would read Alassa, guessing at a place near Gortyna; Ellicott reports ruins two hours' walk away under Cape Leonda still locally so called; Robertson says no ancient writer names either place. Wesley sums it up: the Fair Havens keep their name, but Lasea is utterly lost, with many more of the hundred cities for which Crete was renowned.
9:
The note of time is the hinge, and they all reach for the calendar. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley identify the Fast as the day of atonement on the tenth of Tisri, which Wesley dates to the twenty-fifth of September and Ellicott to the twenty-fourth; Robertson makes it the fifth of October. Ellicott adds that the Jewish sailing season ran from Pentecost to Tabernacles, five days after the Fast, and infers from Luke's naming the one and not the other that the week between them is meant. Robertson has the ancients count the sea unsafe from October until mid-March, and thinks they left Caesarea in August, in ample time to have reached Rome had the winds served. Ellicott guesses that the date stuck in Luke's memory because Paul kept the day, however little he cared to impose it on others; Robertson finds nothing strange in a Gentile writer dating by a Jewish fast, since Paul does the same. Calvin argues the point at length, rejecting the four fasts appointed after the captivity and refusing to refer the word to hunger, wheat being still in the ship.

Whether the warning was prophecy divides them. Gill has it plainly from a spirit of prophecy, by which Paul foresaw and foretold. Ellicott finds the tone that of a man speaking from observation rather than supernatural foresight, and remembers the three shipwrecks behind him and an acquaintance with Crete, shown later in the letter to Titus, close enough that he may have known the harbour. Robertson likewise says he does not here claim prophecy, three wrecks being warrant enough for apprehension. Barnes and Clarke will not choose: the knowledge might have come from the season and the look of an unfit ship, yet nothing forbids believing the Spirit guided him. Robertson thinks it remarkable that a prisoner should venture advice at all and keep venturing it. Robertson notes that the term for hurt is properly an insult, which Josephus uses of the violence of the elements. Both observe that no lives were in fact lost, Ellicott referring that to the prayer Paul made when his counsel was rejected, Robertson to God's mercy for his sake and not to the officers' wisdom.

The two seamen are hard to tell apart. Gill wonders whether one man or two is meant, and describes the governor as sitting aloft in the stern at the helm, giving orders others executed, his skill lying in the stars, the winds, and the sands. Barnes makes the master the helmsman and the owner a separate man holding command as proprietor; Clarke has the proprietor command ship and crew while the pilot guides her under him; Ellicott prefers pilot for the first, the word used of the shipmaster in the Revelation. Robertson reports that the papyri always give the second word the sense of captain rather than owner, and sets the centurion above both, answerable for soldiers, prisoners and cargo, and afraid of being blamed at Rome for timidity when the wheat was wanted. Ellicott thinks it natural that he should trust the experts rather than the enthusiastic Rabbi in his charge. Calvin will not have him reproved: what else should he have done, deferring to Paul in other things but knowing him unskilled in sailing, and almost compelled by a haven not fit to winter in? To yield to the expert is the part of a modest man, and the pilot proposed no venture into the open sea but a run to the next port, almost in view. Luke sets it down, he says, that we may know Paul was furnished from the first with the sense of the Spirit and saw further than the masters, whether by oracle or secret inspiration we cannot tell. Wesley states the rule and the exception together: believe a craftsman in his own craft, yet at the greatest need a real Christian will often advise better.
12:
The haven's unfitness is agreed, though they weigh it differently. Gill suspects the name was given by antiphrasis, a summer road with nothing to break the sea in foul weather; Barnes calls it anchorage for a squall, not a permanent harbour; Ellicott says it sheltered them from the north-westers but lay open elsewhere; Robertson renders the phrase unfit for wintering, a compound occurring nowhere else. Both Ellicott and Robertson take the decision for a formal vote, Robertson calling it a council of the ship's officers on the question Paul had raised, their reasoning being to go on the chance that they might get through. Barnes reads the result the other way, thinking the majority agreed with Paul that the open sea should not be attempted before winter was over, the run to Phenice contradicting nothing. Henry weighs the motives: bleak lying in winter, provisions perhaps scarce and dear, and men running upon a mischief to avoid an inconvenience, as we often do. Some were for staying where they were rather than venturing with the weather so uncertain — better safe in an incommodious harbour than lost in a tempestuous sea — but they were outvoted.

Which harbour, and which way it faced, is the chief dispute. Clarke identifies the two winds as the libs, named from Libya, and the chorus or caurus, quoting Virgil's line on the north-westers ever blowing cold. Barnes takes the words for the harbour's own bearings and reconstructs a curved inlet entered from the south-west and turning to the north-west, proof against wind and sea alike; Wesley says the same more shortly, a haven with a double opening. Ellicott denies the approach: the words are names of winds and not points of the compass, and the harbour is described as looking down them, in the direction they blow, so that it faced north-east and south-east. On that reading he identifies it with the modern Lutro, which Ptolemy names and which Greek pirates use still. Robertson sets the two constructions side by side and admits the choice turns on a preposition: read as facing the wind it yields one site, read as down the line of the wind the other. He follows Ramsay to Lutro, on the ground that sailors describe a harbour as it looks to them going in.

Ellicott adds a stone in evidence. A votive tablet from the reign of Nerva, found near the spot, was raised by an agent of the fleet with an Alexandrian pilot — the word is Luke's own — from which he infers that a corn ship had wintered at that very harbour and left the tablet in thanks for coming through. Henry turns from the place to the sailing. They set out with the south wind blowing softly and kept close along the coast without fear of rock or quicksand; but men who put to sea with the fairest gale do not know what they may meet, and must not reckon the point gained. Here, he says, they looked at second causes and read the smiling wind as a promise, crediting it above the word of God in Paul's mouth. What came was not merely contrary but violent, a wind God commanded out of his treasuries to bring glory to himself and reputation to his servant; and Henry marks the difference from the storm sent after Jonah, Paul going on in his duty and not running from it. The ship was tossed from wave to wave, and he borrows the psalm — mounting to heaven, going down to the depths, staggering like drunken men at their wits' end. She could not bear up into the wind, so they furled what would only have endangered them and let her drive where the sea carried her. They had been near their quiet haven, he thinks, and pleasing themselves with the thought of wintering there, when it was taken from them.
13:
The gentle wind deceived them. Barnes explains that a headwind from the west had veered south, and though not wholly fair seemed enough to coast by; Ellicott has the pilot and owner conclude that all was smooth sailing and stand across the bay for Phenice, hugging the shore for fear of open water. Robertson says the verb for blowing softly occurs nowhere else, and adds that they were so confident they did not even take up the boat towing astern. Ellicott devotes a note to the adverb for close in shore, which the Vulgate and others mistook for a place-name, so that the versions have them leaving Assos, making for it, or sighting it — though the Assos men know lies far north and no Cretan town of the name exists.

The wind's name and quarter are the great question. Barnes takes it for a hurricane veering about rather than a steady wind from one point, of the sort now called a Levanter, and derives the name from words for wind and wave; Wesley says the same. Clarke follows Shaw, who reconstructed the course from the drift itself and concluded that the wind set first east by north and afterwards nearly east by south, Euroclydon being then what a Levanter is now, a name for any tempest from that arc. Shaw thought the rival reading insupportable; Ellicott, Robertson and the manuscripts pull the other way. Ellicott reports Euro-aquilo from some of the best copies, a hybrid unknown to Greek and Latin writers but fitting the phenomena as east by north, and holds that Euroclydon, if genuine, must be a word Luke heard the sailors use; Robertson reports Page's view that it is a corruption of the other. Ellicott also raises a grammatical difficulty, that the pronoun is feminine where the word for ship is neuter, so that it must refer to Crete: of the three possible senses — that the wind drove them against Crete, blew against it, or rushed down from it — only the last agrees with a gale that carried them southward. Robertson reaches the same result from the case of the pronoun, the Cretan mountains rising above seven thousand feet.

Once caught, they could only run. Gill has the ship snatched up bodily; Ellicott and Robertson both dwell on the phrase for bearing up, literally to look the wind in the eye, a figure the more vivid because Greek vessels carried a painted eye on the prow, as Mediterranean boats still do. Robertson quotes the judgment that the squall left no time to furl the great mainsail. Under the little island — Clauda or Cauda, the Gaudos of the geographers and the modern Gozzo — they used the smooth water. Ellicott sets the order of work: first to get aboard the boat that had been towing, hard both because the vessel would not lie head to wind and because it was probably swamped; Barnes insists the point was not a landing but the boat's rescue. Robertson takes the helps for cables passed under the hull and set up tight on deck, a frapping the more needed in ancient ships because of their heavy mast, and reckons after Smith that thirteen days of such a drift would run very nearly the distance to Malta. Calvin reads it morally. The mariners, having got some way with the weather fair, had derided the warning, as men grow proud when fortune favours them, and were now punished for it; they spared neither cargo nor tackle, and when all was tried they despaired, the dark sky serving them for a grave. God meant by it to make the coming rescue more notable, and left his servant to labour with the rest until he seemed past recovery; and though Luke records no prayer, it is likely that while others cursed heaven and earth he was quietly waiting the Lord's leisure.
17:
The helps are agreed to be cables. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott all describe the practice, still called frapping, of passing a rope under the bow and along the keel and setting both ends up on deck; Barnes and Clarke cite a Spanish man-of-war that took six turns of cable round herself to keep from opening; Ellicott reaches back to the Corcyreans in Thucydides and to a line of Horace on keels that scarcely hold against the sea even when girdled with ropes. What was lowered next divides them. Clarke will not hear of striking or slackening sail, since in such a sea they could have carried none; he passes over the yards and the anchor as useless, and supposes the mast itself was cut away. Barnes takes the same view, that the mast came down as is done in storms still. Ellicott holds the opposite: had they struck sail she would have drifted the way they dreaded, and some canvas was needed to keep her steady, so what came down was the gear, the spars and rigging and above all the heavy yard that made her top-heavy.

Whether the quicksands were a real danger is disputed. Ellicott takes it straight: the Syrtes lay along the African coast, the terror of every Mediterranean sailor, and he quotes Lucan on a place that nature left neither sea nor land; the voyagers knew the gale was setting them that way and dared not run full before it. Barnes adds that the banks shifted with the sea and could not be laid down on any chart. Clarke doubts the apprehension. From the direction of the drift, he says, the ship was never near the African coast, and the fear must be taken generally — men afraid of some shoal because they did not know where they were; it is wrong, he holds, to chart the course as though she had been carried down to the syrts at all. He also takes the Adria of the later verse for the sea about Sicily, on an old scholiast's authority.

Then she began to be emptied. Ellicott calls the word a technical one for throwing a cargo overboard, and argues that the act proves the leak was gaining in spite of the undergirding; Robertson adds that loose grain would shift and make her list, danger enough by itself. Clarke guesses at cumbrous wares spoiling her trim; Barnes and Wesley say only that the heavy goods went over. On the third day it was the furniture. Barnes and Clarke take that for spare anchors, cables and baggage, though Barnes notes that anchors remained; Ellicott says the Greek word is wider than the English and takes in beds and luggage and movables of every kind; Wesley thinks unnecessary masts were cut away. Over the reading of that verse there is a division. Ellicott reports that the better manuscripts have they cast out rather than we, and observes that on the received text the passengers were pressed into the work, showing how urgent the peril was. Robertson prefers the third person and dwells on the phrase with their own hands, a word found nowhere else. What broke them at last was the sky. Gill lists what the ancients read there before the loadstone was known — the sun's rays and colour, the moon's size and hue, and above all the two Bears, the Greeks steering by the greater and the Phoenicians by the lesser. Barnes, Clarke and Wesley make the same point more shortly, that without an observation and without a compass they could not tell where they were going. Ellicott thinks the loss of all hope implies more than the gale — a sprung leak they could not stop, with hunger and exhaustion on top of it; Robertson watches the despair settle like a fog, and asks whether Paul had lost hope with the rest.
21:
The long abstinence was not famine. Gill denies that food was wanting or any religious fast meant, laying it to a nausea bred of the tossing and the fear of death, and chiefly to want of time, every hand being employed on the ship. Clarke reports Wakefield's rendering, that there was a scarcity of provisions, and refuses it: the vessel was a corn ship whose wheat went over only later, so they had food and no appetite, and could hardly have dressed it. Robertson agrees, grain in plenty but seasickness and no fires, the medical writers using this word for loss of appetite. Ellicott adds that with no notion how long to a harbour, two hundred and seventy-six men had been put on short rations; Barnes lays it to the weather, the labour and the apprehension together. Henry, more grimly, thinks they had resolved not to eat until they knew whether they were to live or die.

The standing forth is a turn in the narrative and they treat it as one. Robertson calls the participle a pictorial word which sets the solemnity of the scene before us. Henry observes that through the distress Paul had hidden himself in the crowd and helped throw out the tackling, and that now, a prisoner still, he takes on himself the office of counsellor and comforter. Ellicott reads the silence behind it: while the others broke into wailing, calling every man on his god as the sailors did in Jonah, the apostle had spent those hours communing with God, and comes forward because he knows his prayers are heard. Henry presses the comparison the other way: among these seamen Paul was not, like Jonah among his, the cause of the storm but the comfort in it. Calvin explains the timing. A moderate voice could never have been heard through the first uproar; only when they were weary of working and howling, and sat still in a stupor, could a man be listened to, and Paul deferred his word until then.

The reproof itself divides them. Calvin admits it looks unseasonable, Paul objecting their folly in a matter where they knew, and he knew, that he had no skill; but considering how hard men are to bring to soundness of mind, he judges the rebuke profitable, for his authority would have carried no weight unless they first understood that things had gone ill because they despised him. Chiding by itself is cruel, but tempered with a remedy it becomes part of the medicine. It took no small boldness, he adds, to say they ought to have obeyed, since by that word Paul testified he had ordered nothing rashly but what God prescribed; and though no revelation is recorded then, he knew the Spirit governed him, without which a drowning man's promise of safety would have been ridiculous. Henry finds mercy in it: they would not hear the warning, yet on acknowledging their folly they are met with comfort, God being compassionate to men in misery even when they have brought it on themselves; and most people undo themselves because they do not know when they are well off. Over the last phrase there is a real division. Barnes and Clarke grant that it is odd English to speak of gaining a loss but hold the version exact, the Greek covering acquisition of good or evil, Clarke distinguishing the harm done the vessel from the lost cargo. Ellicott would render it to have been spared, arguing from parallels that to gain a harm is to escape it, and notes that the Geneva glossed it so while Tyndale and Cranmer took it as English readers still do. Robertson reports the same dispute, the Revised Version carrying the negative over to the verb while Page and Thayer insist a man is said in Greek to gain a loss when, being in danger of it, he keeps clear.
22:
The change of tone is the first thing noticed. Robertson observes that Paul had himself foretold loss of life as likely, and now gives his reason for a changed view. Barnes and Clarke remark how welcome such news would be to men from whom all hope had been taken, Barnes adding that his earlier counsel had proved wise. Ellicott dwells on the manner rather than the matter: look and tone must have helped, and in a scene of that misery it was something to see one man stand out with a quiet confidence that struck them before ever they heard the grounds of it. Gill supposes the vision came in a dream, or more likely while Paul was awake at prayer. Ellicott contrasts him with others of an enthusiastic cast, in whom visions of the unseen world commonly breed terror, where in Paul they are a source of calm strength he can pass on to other men.

Calvin turns to the risk of being thought rash. Paul promises so absolutely that all shall be saved that he must bring God forward as his witness; and Calvin is confident there was no fear of Satan's counterfeits here, since God never appeared to his servants without plain tokens and the discernment not to be deceived. He sees a further purpose in the naming: Paul extols his God among profane men, that they may learn not only that the true God is worshipped in Judea but that this prisoner worships him — and since they knew why he was in bonds, they might gather from an angel's coming down to him that his cause was approved above. There is in the words, he says, a secret commendation of the gospel, and a kind of triumph in his chains that he should be the minister of safety to so many and the interpreter of God. Clarke reads the design outward: to speak so confidently when every appearance was against him argued full persuasion, and the exactness with which the event answered the prediction must have shown these heathen that Paul's God was other than theirs. Ellicott takes the phrase for one of worship rather than labour, and Wesley calls it a short compendium of religion holding faith, hope and love together.

What the angel granted is weighed carefully. Ellicott takes the charge not to fear as answering a prayer prompted not by fear of death but by dread that the purpose of a lifetime should fail on the verge of attainment, and notes that what follows shows the prayer reached beyond himself. Barnes insists the gift means preservation and not conversion. Clarke counts the two hundred and seventy-six saved for one man's sake a proof of God's approbation, which must have shown the centurion his prisoner was innocent. Wesley presses it further — ask for souls and they shall be given, more than you hoped for — and observes that the centurion, serving providence without knowing it, afterwards gave Paul the prisoners' lives, so that Paul was in God's sight master and pilot of the ship. Calvin asks how far the saints' integrity can profit the wicked, dismisses the notion that any man is a mediator earning salvation for others by merit, and answers that God has reasons for doing good to the reprobate on the faithful's account, as he blessed Potiphar's house for Joseph's sake. On the promised island Gill and Ellicott agree that the detail was given so that the event might prove no accident; Clarke and Robertson point out that the angel did not name it. Calvin thinks the doubt deliberate, exercising the faith of his servant and proving to the rest that this came from the Spirit and not reason; and he notes drily that even so they did not believe him, since when land opened before them the sailors took it for a mainland and not an isle.
27:
The reckoning is settled quickly: Gill, Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley count the fourteenth night from the Fair Havens. On Adria they agree against modern usage: Barnes says the ancients gave the name not to the gulf only but to the whole sea between Greece, Italy and Africa, while Ellicott adds that Josephus, wrecked on the same run two years later, was picked up in the middle of Adria by a ship out of Cyrene. How they guessed at land divides them. Clarke offers the smell of it, which seamen catch at a distance; Ellicott and Robertson fix on the sound of breakers, and Ellicott names the Point of Koura. Gill describes the ancient lead, filled with grease to bring up the bottom and tell rock from sand; Ellicott and Robertson note that a ship passing Koura today takes twenty fathoms and then fifteen.

Four anchors out of the stern is the detail they linger over. Ellicott says such a complement was ordinary, Caesar describing his ships as secured with four apiece. He and Robertson both note that the usual practice is to anchor by the bows, and both bring in the same witness: Nelson anchored by the stern at Copenhagen, and is said to have been reading this chapter on the morning of the battle. Robertson gives the seamanship — anchored from the prow she would have swung round and snapped her cables or presented her stern to the beach — and Ellicott the effect, that she now lay still and would be found at daybreak head to the shore. Gill has them dreading rocks as the depth fell from twenty to fifteen; Barnes says they wanted daylight to see their danger, and Ellicott hears the suspense of that night in Luke's few words.

The sailors' attempt, and Paul's countering of it, carry the weight of the passage. They agree on the trick: the boat was lowered on the pretence of carrying anchors out from the bow, which Ellicott notes would genuinely have required it, while the real design was to reach shore and leave the rest to their fate. Clarke observes that the apostle, depending simply on God's promise, was the one watching over everybody's safety; Gill notices that Paul addressed the soldiers rather than the master and owner, likely in the plot. Then comes the difficulty. Calvin puts it plainly: it is a marvel that Paul should say the rest could not be saved unless the sailors stayed, as if it lay in their power to void God's promise. His answer is that Paul is not separating God's power from his will and the means, since God does not commend his power so that men may sit still and despise them; had Hezekiah opened the gates to the enemy after the promise of deliverance, Isaiah would have cried that he was destroying himself and the city. God's hand is not tied to means, but when he appoints one he holds men's senses within the bounds he has set. Barnes carries it over into salvation: the certainty of an event is no reason against using means, the end being no more determined than the means, so that the decrees bred no neglect in Paul but the strongest exertion. Ellicott refuses to embarrass himself with the question, the promise being realised not by a blind fatalism but by man's co-operation; and Robertson observes that Paul had no notion of lying supinely down and leaving God to do it. Henry adds that duty is ours and events God's, and that we do not trust God but tempt him when we claim his protection without using the means we have. Wesley notices the pronoun: Paul says ye cannot be saved, not we. The soldiers cut the ropes, which Clarke thinks a mark of accuracy, since they alone would have dared cross the crew; Ellicott warns that sullen workers were a new danger.
33:
None of them will take the fortnight's fast literally. Barnes says it cannot mean they had lived without food, only that danger and work left no room for a regular meal. Clarke asks what appetite men could have with death before them. Ellicott is most exact: the word is not the one used for entire abstinence, and it was physically impossible for two hundred and seventy-six men to go a fortnight without eating; scanty rations must have been doled out, but the suspense was such that nobody sat down to a meal. Calvin admits it looks absurd — one man might fast long, but it is scarce credible of so great a multitude — and answers that an unwonted abstinence is improperly called fasting, since they never filled their belly in all that time, men in sorrow almost loathing food. Wesley turns it round: if a sense of present danger makes men forget to eat, we need not wonder when a sense of everlasting danger does the same, nor call that madness which may be the beginning of wisdom.

What Paul urges is bodily strength, and the word for it is disputed. Ellicott argues that the noun means safety rather than health, the translators using the older, wider English sense. Robertson agrees that the word is safety and not spiritual salvation. Wesley puts it bluntly, that they would swim ashore the better for it. Barnes and Clarke identify the promise about the hair as proverbial, and Ellicott repeats that the assurance was not independent of their own co-operation. Ellicott reads the proposal as more than practical insight: soldiers and sailors needed drawing together after the affair of the boat, and what they wanted was food for the body and company for the mind.

Over the bread itself they divide. Gill flatly denies that this was the Lord's supper, and takes it for the common bread of seafaring men, cataloguing ancient ships' provisions to show what such a meal was. Clarke agrees: Paul would not celebrate such a mystery among ungodly sailors and soldiers, Jews and heathens together. Barnes and Robertson take it for the ordinary grace of a Hebrew household, Barnes remarking that Paul, among men who were not Christians, was not ashamed to own his dependence on God, Robertson supposing that he and his friends had memories of the supper where the rest saw only a meal. Ellicott goes furthest: it was no more in itself than the natural incident of eating, but for the few Christians aboard it must have recalled the solemn breaking of bread, and would have been a feast of charity if not strictly eucharistic. Calvin values it as example: the thanksgiving was not merely his daily custom but a testimony of confidence, and he called on God aloud that men drenched in sorrow might catch some hope — and so far succeeded that those who had forgotten through fear to care for their lives took food. On the number Robertson notes that one great manuscript reads about rather than two hundred, but blames a scribe, and observes that Josephus sailed to Italy with six hundred aboard. Ellicott finds it a striking sight, all of them under the influence of one brave spirit. Calvin wants the figure recorded for the miracle's sake: few but the sailors could swim, they were worn past moving their arms, and it is seldom that twenty swim in danger without one drowning another. The last jettison closes it. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott agree the wheat went to lighten her so she might run in closer, Ellicott suggesting it was what had been kept back for provisions, the object being only to keep her afloat till they reached land. Calvin sees in it proof that Paul had at last prevailed, since it was still dark and no haven known — though, all unbelievers being unstable, the persuasion soon wore off.
39:
That they did not know the land is explained rather than excused. Barnes supposes they had been driven without one observation and were strangers to the island; Ellicott and Robertson give the better reason, that some of the sailors had likely been at Malta before, but the bay lay well away from the great harbour where shipping went. Robertson reads the tense as an attempt: they tried to recognise it and could not. On the creek they are agreed in substance. Barnes renders it a bay and says the point of naming its shore is that the landing was level, not a face of rock; Ellicott adds that the word means a flat sandy beach in Homer. Ellicott and Robertson note that the verb for thrusting the ship in is a sailor's term for running her aground.

The three operations of getting under way are described in detail. On the anchors Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott all prefer the sense of cutting the cables and leaving the anchors in the sea, Ellicott arguing that nothing was gained by burdening a ship they wanted light. On the rudder-bands they agree and are unusually specific. Barnes notes that the Greek word is plural, and Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott describe two paddle-like blades, one on each quarter, hoisted out of the water and lashed while the ship lay useless, so that loosing the bands let them fall back. The sail divides them. Clarke denies it can be the mainsail, which would have been improper here, and makes it the jib run from the foremast to the bowsprit. Ellicott, whose word survives in the Italian for a ship's largest sail, points out that in ancient rigging the largest was the foresail; Robertson agrees, and adds that the word for wind is a participle, the breeze that was blowing, which seems to imply the gale had slackened.

Where they struck is a matter of local knowledge. Gill and Barnes take the phrase for an isthmus washed on both sides, Barnes adding that it can hardly have been above water, being more likely a sandbank they never saw. Ellicott and Robertson agree on the topography: at the west end of the bay lies a small island the crew could not have known was one, and making for the beach they grounded on the bank between it and the coast, where two currents meet. Clarke admits that the nautical terms of this chapter are extremely difficult, and that he cannot be sure of having hit the sense everywhere. The prow was fixed — Robertson's verb means fastened firmly, the adjective unshakeable — while the stern was being broken up, the tense in Ellicott and Robertson alike expressing an action still going on. Barnes finds a mercy in it, the stern furnishing the boards on which the company got ashore. Calvin takes the sharpest view. It might seem then that God had mocked his servant and Paul fed his fellow passengers on an empty hope; but God removed the error by prospering them, and it was fitting that their hearts should melt when the ship went to pieces, since despair increases the glory of a miracle. He governs his works so as to make some show of difficulty, until we learn that he will have the victory though all the world strive against him; and so he chose rather to draw them ashore from a wreck than bring the ship in whole. Henry turns it to the reader: the vessel that rode out the storm in open water is dashed to pieces the moment she sticks fast, as a heart fixed in the world is lost while a heart kept above it, however tossed, has hope. They had the shore in sight and were wrecked in the harbour, which teaches us never to be secure; yet whatever the difficulty, a promised salvation shall without fail be brought to pass.
42:
Why the soldiers wanted the prisoners dead is answered two ways; Ellicott and Robertson point to Roman law, which put a guard's life in forfeit if his charge escaped, so that in killing them the soldiers saw their only chance of not being killed; Barnes offers the same reason but adds that they probably counted on its being taken for a drowning, and draws from it that men can be cruel in the very hour of God's mercy. Clarke has no patience with them: bloodthirsty and cowardly villains, whose trade was in human blood, who had watched these poor men bear the same distresses as themselves and now, when all who could swim might reach land, wanted them massacred lest they should. Wesley disposes of it in three words: cruel, unjust, ungrateful. Calvin makes ingratitude the charge. They had Paul to thank twice over for their lives, and were now minded to kill the man for whose sake they should have spared the others; he had saved them like an angel of God and refreshed them on the day they were past hope, and they stick at nothing to destroy him.

Calvin sees a worse fault under the first. They had received the oracle that all their souls were given to Paul, and now, expecting to be saved with him dead, what are they doing but resisting God? The grace they tasted unwillingly in their extremity had lost its relish the moment the harbour came in sight. But he bids us mark the counsel of God, who both saved his servant and kept his promise by bringing to land the very men who did what they could to make it void — his goodness striving so with human wickedness. On the centurion the others are agreed. Barnes traces his kindness from the start of the voyage, through the advice at Fair Havens and his prudence in the storm, and perhaps a belief that Paul stood under divine protection; Clarke thinks he had seen the man was not only innocent but extraordinary; Gill adds the deeper reason, that a superior influence moved him, so that the word about Rome should stand. Barnes draws the lesson that benefit comes to sinners through the righteous, as ten would have saved Sodom; Robertson says the centurion knew by now how much they owed him.

The order of the landing is noticed as a piece of command. Ellicott observes that this was no rush of every man for himself: the centurion kept his head and could enforce discipline, sending the swimmers first to be on the beach ready to help the rest, and guesses that Paul, three times shipwrecked, was among them and may have suggested it. Clarke thinks the soldiers all got ashore that way, Roman training including how to swim, and notes that the prisoners were loosed. For the rest it was planks and whatever came off the ship — Robertson noting that the word for plank occurs nowhere else, the breaking up of the stern having furnished the timber. Clarke will not let the escape pass as ordinary: with the surf still violent, how should the sick and the aged have come ashore on planks they had no skill to steer? Barnes and Robertson take the outcome as the promise fulfilled, Robertson calling the narrative worthy of any historian in any age. Clarke closes the chapter with the reflection that the malice of the Jews and the fury of the elements were alike overruled, so that governors and nobles heard the gospel who otherwise would not, and Malta received it by way of a wreck; and that assurance of God's will never excuses human means, Paul himself looking for a blessing on men's care. Wesley hopes that some who came ashore received the apostle as a teacher sent from God, and found in that day's deliverance the earnest of a greater one.
